title: Linear Graphs & Functions
description: Plotting coordinates, gradient, y-intercept, the equation y=mx+c, and parallel and perpendicular lines.

notes.heading: Plotting Points on the Cartesian Plane
notes.body:
Every point on the Cartesian plane is located by an ordered pair $(x,y)$.

📌 Definition
The Cartesian plane is formed by two perpendicular number lines called axes. The horizontal axis is the $x$-axis and the vertical axis is the $y$-axis. They cross at the origin $(0,0)$.

🔑 Key Concept
The first coordinate tells you how far to move horizontally; the second tells you how far to move vertically. The plane is divided into four quadrants:
1. Quadrant I: $x>0$, $y>0$
2. Quadrant II: $x<0$, $y>0$
3. Quadrant III: $x<0$, $y<0$
4. Quadrant IV: $x>0$, $y<0$

💡 Worked Example
Plot the points $A(2,3)$, $B(-1,4)$, $C(-3,-2)$ and $D(4,-1)$.
• $A$ is 2 right and 3 up → Quadrant I.
• $B$ is 1 left and 4 up → Quadrant II.
• $C$ is 3 left and 2 down → Quadrant III.
• $D$ is 4 right and 1 down → Quadrant IV.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always write coordinates as $(x,y)$; order matters.
• Points on the $x$-axis have $y=0$; points on the $y$-axis have $x=0$.
• The origin $(0,0)$ is in no quadrant.

✅ Check
To verify a plotted point, count from the origin along the $x$-axis first, then parallel to the $y$-axis.

notes.heading: Gradient of a Straight Line
notes.body:
The gradient measures how steep a straight line is.

📌 Definition
The gradient $m$ between two points $(x_1,y_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2)$ is:
$$m=\dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$$

🔑 How it works
• Positive gradient: the line rises as $x$ increases.
• Negative gradient: the line falls as $x$ increases.
• Zero gradient: the line is horizontal.
• Undefined gradient: the line is vertical.

💡 Worked Example
Find the gradient of the line through $A(2,5)$ and $B(6,13)$.
Step 1: Label $(x_1,y_1)=(2,5)$ and $(x_2,y_2)=(6,13)$.
Step 2: Substitute:
$$m=\dfrac{13-5}{6-2}=\dfrac{8}{4}=2$$
So the gradient is $2$: for every 1 unit right, the line rises 2 units.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Mixing the order of the points. Use the same point order in the numerator and denominator:
$$m=\dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}=\dfrac{y_1-y_2}{x_1-x_2}$$
Both are correct if consistent.

notes.heading: The Equation $y=mx+c$
notes.body:
Every non-vertical straight line can be written in slope-intercept form.

📌 Definition
$$y=mx+c$$
where $m$ is the gradient and $c$ is the $y$-intercept, the value of $y$ where the line crosses the $y$-axis.

🔑 How it works
To sketch a line from its equation:
1. Mark the $y$-intercept $(0,c)$.
2. Use the gradient to find another point: from $(0,c)$, move 1 unit right and $m$ units up (or down if $m$ is negative).
3. Join the points with a straight line.

💡 Worked Example
Sketch $y=2x+3$.
• The $y$-intercept is $(0,3)$.
• The gradient is $2$, so move 1 right and 2 up to $(1,5)$.
• Draw the line through $(0,3)$ and $(1,5)$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $m$ controls steepness and direction.
• $c$ controls where the line crosses the $y$-axis.
• Lines with the same $c$ meet the $y$-axis at the same point.

✅ Tip
Rewrite the equation with $y$ as the subject before reading $m$ and $c$.

notes.heading: Finding the Equation of a Line
notes.body:
You can find the equation of a line from different pieces of information.

📌 Key Concept
If you know the gradient $m$ and one point $(x_1,y_1)$, use point-slope form:
$$y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$$
Then rearrange to $y=mx+c$.

If you know two points, first find the gradient, then substitute one point to find $c$.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Gradient and a point
Find the equation of the line with gradient $3$ through $(2,7)$.
$$y-7=3(x-2)$$
$$y-7=3x-6$$
$$y=3x+1$$

💡 Worked Example 2 — Two points
Find the equation of the line through $(1,4)$ and $(3,10)$.
Step 1: Gradient:
$$m=\dfrac{10-4}{3-1}=\dfrac{6}{2}=3$$
Step 2: Substitute into $y=mx+c$ using $(1,4)$:
$$4=3(1)+c \Rightarrow c=1$$
Step 3: Equation:
$$y=3x+1$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The final answer is usually given as $y=mx+c$.
• Either point can be used to find $c$.
• Check by substituting the other point.

⚠️ Common Misconception
Forgetting to add $y_1$ back when rearranging $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$.

notes.heading: Parallel and Perpendicular Lines
notes.body:
Parallel and perpendicular lines have special gradient relationships.

📌 Definition
Two lines are parallel if they never meet. Parallel lines have the same gradient:
$$m_1=m_2$$
Two lines are perpendicular if they meet at a right angle. Their gradients satisfy:
$$m_1 \times m_2=-1$$
So each gradient is the negative reciprocal of the other.

🔑 How it works
If a line has gradient $m$:
• A parallel line also has gradient $m$.
• A perpendicular line has gradient $-\dfrac{1}{m}$.

💡 Worked Example 1
For $y=4x-5$:
• A parallel line is $y=4x+2$ (gradient $4$).
• A perpendicular line is $y=-\dfrac{1}{4}x+3$ (gradient $-\dfrac{1}{4}$).

💡 Worked Example 2
Show the line through $(0,2)$ and $(2,8)$ is perpendicular to the line through $(0,5)$ and $(3,4)$.
Gradient 1:
$$m_1=\dfrac{8-2}{2-0}=3$$
Gradient 2:
$$m_2=\dfrac{4-5}{3-0}=-\dfrac{1}{3}$$
Product:
$$m_1 \times m_2=3 \times \left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)=-1$$
Therefore the lines are perpendicular.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Parallel lines share the same gradient but have different $y$-intercepts.
• The negative reciprocal of $\dfrac{a}{b}$ is $-\dfrac{b}{a}$.
• Horizontal lines are perpendicular to vertical lines.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Thinking perpendicular gradients are just negatives of each other. They are negative reciprocals, so $m_2=-\dfrac{1}{m_1}$, not $m_2=-m_1$.

notes.heading: Horizontal and Vertical Lines
notes.body:
Some lines are not described by $y=mx+c$.

📌 Definition
A horizontal line has equation $y=c$ and gradient $0$.
A vertical line has equation $x=a$ and an undefined gradient.

🔑 How it works
For $y=c$, every point has the same $y$-coordinate, so:
$$m=\dfrac{0}{x_2-x_1}=0$$
For $x=a$, every point has the same $x$-coordinate, so:
$$m=\dfrac{y_2-y_1}{0} \text{ (undefined)}$$

💡 Worked Example
Write the equation of:
1. The horizontal line through $(5,-2)$: $y=-2$.
2. The vertical line through $(5,-2)$: $x=5$.
The two lines intersect at $(5,-2)$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Horizontal lines are parallel to the $x$-axis.
• Vertical lines are parallel to the $y$-axis.
• $y=mx+c$ cannot describe a vertical line.

✅ Tip
When reading a graph, look for perfectly flat or upright lines and state their equations carefully.

notes.heading: Modelling with Linear Relationships
notes.body:
Many real-world situations change at a constant rate and can be modelled by a straight line.

📌 Definition
A linear model has the form $y=mx+c$, where:
• $m$ is the rate of change.
• $c$ is the initial value or fixed value when $x=0$.

🔑 How it works
Identify the input variable ($x$) and output variable ($y$). The gradient tells you how much $y$ changes for each one-unit increase in $x$.

💡 Worked Example
A phone plan costs £15 per month plus £2 for each gigabyte of data used.
Let $g$ be the number of GB used and $C$ be the total monthly cost.
$$C=2g+15$$
• The gradient $2$ means each extra GB costs £2.
• The intercept $15$ is the fixed monthly charge.
If a customer uses $8$ GB:
$$C=2(8)+15=16+15=31$$
The bill is £31.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The gradient represents a rate such as cost per unit, distance per hour, or pay per hour.
• The $y$-intercept represents a starting amount or fixed fee.
• Test your model with simple values to check it makes sense.

⚠️ Common Misconception
Confusing the fixed value with the rate. In $C=2g+15$, the £15 is paid even if no data is used; the £2 is added per GB.

questions.stem: In which quadrant does the point $(-3,4)$ lie?
questions.explanation: Negative $x$ and positive $y$ place a point in Quadrant II.

questions.stem: What is the gradient of the line through $(1,2)$ and $(5,10)$?
questions.explanation: Gradient measures the steepness of a line: it tells you how much the $y$-value changes for each one-unit increase in $x$. Using the points $(1,2)$ and $(5,10)$, the change in $y$ is $10-2=8$ and the change in $x$ is $5-1=4$, so $m=\dfrac{8}{4}=2$. In real life, a gradient of 2 is like a ramp that rises 2 metres for every 1 metre horizontally.

questions.stem: A line has gradient $-2$ and passes through $(0,5)$. What is its equation?
questions.explanation: The $y$-intercept is $5$ and the gradient is $-2$, so $y=-2x+5$.

questions.stem: Find the equation of the line through $(2,5)$ and $(4,11)$.

questions.explanation: Parallel lines have the same gradient, so the answer must keep $m=\dfrac{2}{3}$.

questions.stem: A line is perpendicular to $y=5x+2$. What is its gradient?
What is the equation of the horizontal line through $(6,-2)$?
questions.explanation: A horizontal line has equation $y=c$, so through $(6,-2)$ it is $y=-2$.

questions.stem: The line through $(0,c)$ and $(4,14)$ has gradient $2$. Find $c$.
A plumber charges a £40 call-out fee plus £25 per hour. Which equation gives the total cost $C$ for $h$ hours?
questions.explanation: The £40 is the fixed intercept and £25 is the rate per hour, so $C=25h+40$.
Rearranging gives $y=3x+4$, gradient $3$; a perpendicular gradient is $-\dfrac{1}{3}$.

questions.stem: Find the equation of the line through $(-1,5)$ that is parallel to $y=2x+3$.
questions.explanation: Parallel means $m=2$. Substituting $(-1,5)$ gives $5=-2+c$, so $c=7$ and $y=2x+7$.

questions.stem: The points $(2,a)$ and $(6,1)$ lie on a line with gradient $-\dfrac{3}{4}$. Find $a$.
A car rental company charges £30 per day plus a one-off £20 insurance fee. What is the cost of a 7-day rental?
questions.explanation: Using $C=30d+20$ with $d=7$ gives $C=210+20=230$, so the cost is £230.
